name: Interstellar's Wormhole
description: The wormhole Oliver James, Eugénie von Tunzelmann, Paul Franklin, and Kip Thorne designed for Christopher Nolan's film Interstellar of 2014, which they call the Dneg wormhole after the effects studio Double Negative. A cylinder of length $2a$, every sphere along it of radius $\rho$, joins two flat spaces, each through a mouth that flares out over a length set by $M$, and clocks everywhere keep the same time, $g_{tt} = -1$.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $\rho$, $a$, and $M$ are lengths. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: In Christopher Nolan's film Interstellar of 2014 a wormhole floats near Saturn, a sphere in which the stars and nebulae of a distant galaxy can be seen [nolan2014interstellar, james2015]. Nolan's request, in May 2013, was for images of it and of a fast spinning black hole at the resolution and smoothness of IMAX [james2015]. The work fell to Kip Thorne, a physicist at Caltech and an executive producer of the film, and to Oliver James, Eugénie von Tunzelmann, and Paul Franklin of the effects studio Double Negative in London [james2015]. Together the four wrote a code that traces light through curved spacetime, the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer [james2015, james2015lensing]. For students they set out a recipe for tracing the rays, and Thorne, by the four authors' own account "a total klutz at numerical work", carried it out in Mathematica [james2015]. Wormholes had been on screen before, in Star Trek and Stargate among others, but by the four authors' account none had been shown as a nearby human would see one [james2015].¶Thorne had written about wormholes before: in 1988, in connection with Carl Sagan's novel Contact, he and Michael Morris offered them as a tool for teaching general relativity [james2015, morris1988]. The wormhole of the textbooks, James Hartle's among them, was the drainhole Homer Ellis published in 1973, $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + d\ell^2 + (\rho^2 + \ell^2)\,d\Omega^2$, one throat of radius $\rho$ between two flat spaces [ellis1973, james2015]. Morris and Thorne had written down the same metric without knowing of Ellis's paper, and in 2015 they apologized for the missing credit [james2015]. Nolan wanted to see how a wormhole's look depends on its shape, and Ellis's has one shape at every size, so the team designed a wormhole with three free parameters [james2015].¶Its middle is a tube of length $2a$ along which every sphere has the radius $\rho$, and at each end of the tube a mouth opens into a flat space, sharp edged in a first version and smoothly flared in the one the film used [james2015]. They chose the flare, "somewhat arbitrarily", to have "approximately the same form as that from the throat (horizon) of a nonspinning black hole to the external universe in which the hole lives" [james2015]. Beyond the mouth $\ell = a$ the radius grows as $r = \rho + M(x\arctan x - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 + x^2))$ with $x = 2(\ell - a)/\pi M$, so that $dr/d\ell = \tfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan x$ climbs from $0$ at the mouth toward $1$ far away [james2015]. A black hole's throat has the radius $2M$, and here $\rho$ and $M$ are set free of each other, so that $M$ fixes only how gently the mouth flares [james2015]. Embedded in flat space, the equator of one moment is a tube with two flared ends, and the team called the distance across which a flare turns from vertical to $45°$ its lensing width, $W = 1.42953\,M$ [james2015].¶How long should a wormhole be, and how wide its flare? Through a long one a camera sees Saturn again and again, each new image carried by light that wraps once more around the tube, and a wide flare bends the light of the stars around the mouth into second and third images [james2015]. Nolan chose a very short wormhole, $2a = 0.01\rho$, since for greater lengths "the multiple images would be confusing to a mass audience" [james2015]. For the lensing width he took $W = 0.05\rho$, enough to be interesting and far less than a black hole's, so that the wormhole would look unlike Gargantua, the film's black hole [james2015]. The radius $\rho$ he set at one kilometre, which makes the wormhole's lensing of the stars of our galaxy visible from Earth with the technology of the film's era, "but barely so" [james2015].¶A wormhole with $g_{tt} = -1$ pulls on nothing, and the slow approach Nolan asked for, which gives the audience time to look before Cooper, the pilot, takes the Endurance in, needed a pull of about Earth's, $10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ or less [james2015]. So the team added a weak Newtonian potential $\Phi$ to the time part of the metric, at most about $10^{-12}$ of $c^2$, which slows clocks near the mouth by no more than a part in $10^{12}$ [james2015]. It is far too weak to bend light visibly, so the rays can be traced with $\Phi = 0$ [james2015]. Just outside the edge of the wormhole's image lies its Einstein ring, the image of a point directly behind it on the camera's side, and as the camera moves, two images of a star near the ring race around it in opposite directions, one just inside and one just outside [james2015].¶Through the wormhole Nolan chose, the trip was quick and dull to watch, and through a long one it looked like the tunnels of earlier films [james2015]. The sequence on screen mixes the code's views of the interior with effects animation made from aerial photographs of dramatic landscapes [james2015]. Holding any such wormhole open takes exotic matter, with a negative energy density in some frames, and the quantum inequalities on negative energy, once strengthened, will probably keep one this large from staying open long enough to cross: "Likely, but not certain" [james2015, morris1988]. The team worked as if they were "engineers in some arbitrarily advanced civilization" whose construction crews could build any wormhole geometry [james2015].

related.text: The general static wormhole of Michael Morris and Kip Thorne. In its proper distance chart with $\Phi = 0$ and the areal radius chosen as the team chose it for the film, it is this wormhole [james2015, morris1988].
The wormhole the team began from and set aside: Ellis's throat has one shape at every size, and Christopher Nolan wanted a shape he could adjust [james2015].
Along its cylinder, $|\ell| \le a$, this wormhole is the product of the flat plane of $t$ and $\ell$ with a sphere of radius $\rho$, Plebański and Hacyan's flat plane times a sphere with $b = \rho$.

As $M \to 0$ the flares sharpen into edges, and with $a = 0$ as well this wormhole becomes two flat spaces, each with a ball of radius $\rho$ cut out, joined across the edges, which is Visser's thin shell wormhole with no mass [james2015, visser1989prd].
Each mouth flares out roughly as space opens out from Schwarzschild's horizon, with $M$ in the part of the mass, and the mouth's radius $\rho$ left free where the horizon's is $2M$ [james2015].
Gargantua, the black hole of the same film, drawn from Kerr's metric by the same team with the same code [james2015lensing].

coordinates.name: Proper Distance

parameters.description: Areal radius, a length: $r = \rho$ on the cylinder $|\ell| \le a$, and beyond it $r = \rho + M\left(x\arctan x - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(1 + x^2\right)\right)$ with $x = 2\left(|\ell| - a\right)/\pi M$, so that $r$ and $\partial_\ell r = \tfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan x$ are continuous at the mouths and $\partial_\ell r \to \pm 1$ far away
Radius of the cylinder and of its two mouths, a length
Half the length of the cylinder, a length; the mouths are the spheres $\ell = \pm a$

Length over which each mouth flares out into flat space, the part a black hole's mass plays for its horizon; the lensing width, the distance across the embedded surface over which it turns from vertical to $45°$, is $W = 1.42953\,M$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \ell, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\ell$ the proper distance along a radial line, zero halfway along the cylinder. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.

parameters.description: Radius of the cylinder and of its two mouths, a length

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \ell, \theta, \phi)$ on the cylinder between the mouths, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\ell$ the proper distance along a radial line from its middle. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.

parameters.description: Radius of the cylinder and of its two mouths, a length

Distance beyond the mouth in units of $\pi M/2$, a pure number
Areal radius, a length, $\rho$ at the mouth and growing as $\ell$ far away

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \ell, \theta, \phi)$ beyond the mouth $\ell = a$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\ell$ the proper distance along a radial line from the middle of the cylinder; the flare beyond $\ell = -a$ is its mirror image under $\ell \to -\ell$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.
